source:
Brit is Gertrude's lady-in-waiting. She can be terribly cruel. We've never gotten along since she came to Elsinore three years ago.

She is the daughter of one of the most powerful noble families in Denmark, as with most of the people here at Elsinore.

布莉特是乔特鲁德的宫廷侍女。她有时刻薄得可怕。自从三年前她来到埃尔西诺，我们就一直合不来。

source: Brit seems convinced that it is Claudius having me killed, because he finds my affection for Hamlet dangerous. It's believable, almost... but if Claudius wanted me dead, he's killed before, and wouldn't send another to do that work. Still, maybe there is something to find there.

source: By turning Lady Brit in to Bernardo, I managed to stop her from killing me this loop. source:
Brit is Gertrude's lady in waiting. She can be terribly cruel. We've never gotten along since she came to Elsinore three years ago.

布莉特是乔特鲁德的宫廷侍女。她刻薄起来十分可怕。自从三年前她来到埃尔西诺，我们就一直合不来。

source: Lady Brit is in the employ of Lord Fortinbras, at her father's behest. That's why she sought to kill me. Destroying me would ensure Laertes was angry enough to dethrone Claudius—at least, that was their hope. I foiled that hope in stopping her plan.

source: Ophelia: Father? Polonius: There's my girl. Laertes: Finally awake, O lazy sister of mine? Gertrude: Ophelia! OooOOOoh, Ophelia!... Hamlet: Uh, you'll have to pardon mother. We all began drinking a... bit much waiting for you to rouse. The wine's been out for hours. Gertrude: I'm so haaaappy! I love a good summer feast. Claudius: Now, love, can we finally begin? I know you wanted to wait for Ophelia. Well, here she is. Let's not let the food grow cold. Guilda: Please. I'm starving to death. I'm not long for this world. Rosie: Guilda, we just had sweetmeats—not an hour ago, too. Guilda: But have you seen the table? Irma outdid herself. I can't wait another second! I'll die! Irma: Finally, someone who likes to eat my food as much as I like to make it. Ophelia: You all are having a party? What of the morning court session? What of Fortinbras? Claudius: Fortinbras? You mean the Prince of Norway? Bernardo: What of him, Ophelia? Ophelia: He... well, the... diplomatic effort. Didn't he... isn't he threatening Denmark? Bernardo: What? Sire, have I missed something? Claudius: I don't think so. I'm not sure what you mean, Ophelia. But I have noticed there's no goblet in your hand. Hmm! Come! Drink! Be merry! And that's a royal order. Hamlet: Er, mother, do you need to be tucked into bed? You're drifting off. Claudius: Don't mind her, Hamlet. Let her sleep if she wants to. She'll wake up as the night goes on. Marcellus: I'll watch over her, m'lord. I'll call for yeh if she wakes! Uh, assumin' I'm not drunk myself. Hamlet: She seems remarkably happy tonight, doesn't she, uncle? The happiest since, well... Since Father's illness took him. Claudius: Aye, she does. I wish his health hadn't declined so quickly. I loved my brother. I wanted him to live. For her sake, and for yours. Hamlet: It wasn't your fault. There was nothing to be done. Plague steals indiscriminately. My father was a good man. And you—you're the closest to him I have now. All will be well in time. Claudius: I'll drink to that, nephew. Ophelia: (This is so strange. Did history itself change?) (Claudius isn't a murderer in this world, at the very least...) Laertes. Aren't you sailing for Paris? Laertes: Oh! About that. for some reason, I couldn't sleep last night, and I got to thinking about it. I believe I'll stay in Elsinore a while longer. There's time enough for travel later on. How often does such a bright, warm summer as this come to visit Denmark, after all? Ophelia: Well, that's wonderful. I'm sure Brit will be very happy, too. Brit: Happy that he's staying? It's not the worst, I suppose. Laertes: (Listen, Ophelia. Just between you and me, I've got a little surprise in mind tonight.) (Wait and see.) Horatio: Come, Ophelia. Let me show you to your seat. Shall we dine? Ophelia: Of course. Laertes: Everyone, I've a toast to make. Gertrude: Hear, hear! Claudius: Of course, Laertes. Laertes: I'd like to toast to health, to life, and to love. And to this brilliant, wonderful woman—whom I love, and who has loved me in return. Brit: Wha? Me? Laertes: To some, our relationship has been known a long time. To others, it may be—er—more of a surprise. Polonius: I'll say. Why have I never heard of this before? Brit: Laertes? Laertes, you don't have to. Laertes: Tonight, I'd like to ask Lady Birgitta for her hand in marriage. Brit: Oh. Gertrude: Ah! Yesh! Yesh! Hamlet: Well, I'll be damned. Certainly took him long enough. Polonius: Laertes! This is highly irregular! Ophelia: Oh, come now, Father. They're a suitable match of sufficient rank. What have you to fear? Polonius: W-well, nothing, but I—I haven't spoken to or met her father, and I haven't asked his mind, and— And well, the dowry, and... Laertes: Brit, I love you. I don't want to travel the world without you. If there's any way you share those feelings... if you think you could... share your life... Brit: I accept, you idiot. Of course. You didn't have to be so public, though. Invite them all into our bedroom too while you're at it, why don't you? Polonius: Hmph. Well then. Let me not to the marriage of true minds admit impediments. If this is your wish, then... We're going to have a wedding! Ophelia: Congratulations, brother. I'm happy to see you happy. Laertes: I must admit, I'm relieved. I wasn't sure how you and Father would take the news. Let's not let the night end. I've already talked to Bernardo and Hamlet. Whenever we can slip away, the three of us are planning to meet by the pond. Ophelia: You want to slip away? But everyone's still here. Laertes: Oh, it's a welcome celebration, but I can only take so much drunk revelry. A quieter venue fits the mood. You should come. It's been so long since the four of us got together. Ophelia: Yes. I'd... I'd like that. I'll be there. This is it. He's gone. I can scarcely believe it. Everything is the way it was meant to be.
target: 奥菲莉娅: 父亲？ 波洛涅斯: 我的好女儿来了。 雷欧提斯: 我这懒妹妹，你终于醒了？ 乔特鲁德: 奥菲莉娅！哦——哦——奥菲莉娅！…… 哈姆雷特: 呃，请你别介意母亲这样。 等你醒来的时候，我们都喝得……有点多了。酒都摆出来好几个小时了。 乔特鲁德: 我好开——心！我最喜欢丰盛的夏日宴席了。 克劳狄斯: 亲爱的，现在总算可以开始了吧？ 我知道你想等奥菲莉娅。好了，她来了。别让饭菜凉了。 吉尔妲: 求你们了。我都快饿死了。没多久可活了。 罗茜: 吉尔达，我们刚吃过甜点——还不到一个小时呢。 吉尔妲: 可你看见桌上的菜了吗？伊尔玛这次比以往做得都好。我一秒也等不了了！我要死了！ 伊尔玛: 终于有人这么爱吃我做的饭，就像我爱做饭一样。 奥菲莉娅: 你们在开宴会？那早上的朝会呢？福丁布拉斯呢？ 克劳狄斯: 福丁布拉斯？你是说挪威王子？ 贝尔纳多: 他怎么了，奥菲莉娅？ 奥菲莉娅: 他……就是，那个……外交交涉。他不是……他不是在威胁丹麦吗？ 贝尔纳多: 什么？陛下，是有什么事我不知道吗？ 克劳狄斯: 我想没有。我不太明白你的意思，奥菲莉娅。不过我倒是注意到，你手里还没拿酒杯。嗯！ 来吧！喝酒！尽情欢乐！这可是国王的命令。 哈姆雷特: 呃，母亲，要送您上床睡觉吗？您都快睡着了。 克劳狄斯: 别管她，哈姆雷特。她想睡就让她睡吧。晚些时候她会醒的。 马塞勒斯: 殿下，我会照看她。她醒了我就叫您！呃，前提是我自己没喝醉。 哈姆雷特: 叔叔，她今晚看起来特别开心，不是吗？自从……嗯，那之后，就没这么开心过。 自从父亲因病去世之后。 克劳狄斯: 是啊，确实。 要是他的身体没有恶化得那么快就好了。我爱我的哥哥。我希望他活着。为了她，也为了你。 哈姆雷特: 这不是您的错。当时谁也无能为力。瘟疫夺人性命，从不挑人。 我父亲是个好人。而您——如今我身边的人里，您与他最亲近。慢慢地，一切都会好起来。 克劳狄斯: 为这话干一杯，我的侄儿。 奥菲莉娅: （这太奇怪了。难道连历史本身都变了？） （至少，在这个世界里，克劳狄斯不是凶手……） 雷欧提斯。你不是要坐船去巴黎吗？ 雷欧提斯: 哦！说到这个。不知为什么，我昨晚睡不着，就想了想这件事。 我想，我还是在埃尔西诺多待一阵吧。以后有的是时间去旅行。 毕竟，丹麦能有几次这样阳光明媚、温暖的夏天呢？ 奥菲莉娅: 那太好了。布莉特肯定也会很高兴。 布莉特: 因为他留下来而高兴？我想，这也不算最坏的事吧。 雷欧提斯: （听着，奥菲莉娅。这事只告诉你，今晚我打算准备一个小惊喜。） （等着瞧吧。） 霍拉旭: 来，奥菲莉娅。我带你入座。我们用餐吧？ 奥菲莉娅: 当然。 雷欧提斯: 各位，我想敬一杯酒。 乔特鲁德: 好啊，好啊！ 克劳狄斯: 当然，雷欧提斯。 雷欧提斯: 我想为健康、生命和爱情举杯。 也敬这位聪慧、美好的女子——我爱她，她也爱着我。 布莉特: 啊？我？ 雷欧提斯: 有些人早就知道我们的关系。对另一些人来说，这可能——呃——更像是个意外。 波洛涅斯: 我可太意外了。 为什么我以前从没听说过这件事？ 布莉特: 雷欧提斯？ 雷欧提斯，你不必这样。 雷欧提斯: 今晚，我想向布莉吉塔女士求婚。 布莉特: 噢。 乔特鲁德: 啊！好哇！好哇！ 哈姆雷特: 哎呀，真没想到。他可算是开口了。 波洛涅斯: 雷欧提斯！这太不合规矩了！ 奥菲莉娅: 哎，父亲，别这样。他们很般配，身份地位也相称。 您有什么好担心的？ 波洛涅斯: 这、这个，没什么，可我——我还没见过她父亲，也没跟他说过话，更没问过他的意见，还有—— 还有，嗯，嫁妆，还有…… 雷欧提斯: 布莉特，我爱你。我不想独自去周游世界。 如果你也有哪怕一点同样的感情……如果你觉得你愿意……与我共度一生…… 布莉特: 我答应，你这个笨蛋。当然答应。不过，你也不用这么当众说出来。 那你怎么不干脆把他们全请进我们的卧室呢？ 波洛涅斯: 哼。那好吧。真心相契的结合，我不该横加阻挠。 如果这是你们的心愿，那么…… 我们要办婚礼了！ 奥菲莉娅: 恭喜你，哥哥。看到你开心，我也很开心。 雷欧提斯: 说实话，我松了口气。我之前不确定你和父亲听到这消息会有什么反应。 别让今晚就这么结束吧。 我已经和贝尔纳多、哈姆雷特说好了。一有机会溜走，我们三个就到池塘边碰面。 奥菲莉娅: 你想溜走？可大家都还在这里呢。 雷欧提斯: 哦，这场庆祝是挺好，可这群醉醺醺的人闹个不停，我也受不了太久。 安静点的地方更合心意。你也来吧。我们四个好久没聚在一起了。 奥菲莉娅: 好。我……我很想去。 我会去的。 就是这样了。 他不在了。我简直不敢相信。一切都成了本该有的样子。

source: Laertes: Bartender, a flagon of the finest, if you please. You must be that one they call Othello. Othello: ...So it would seem. And you must be the one they call Lord Laertes. Laertes: Lord Laertes... it always was a funny title. I suppose I am now a Duke, aren't I? Othello: Unfortunate news about your father, m'lord. Laertes: He was a good man. The best sort of man, a stalwart advisor, and a wonderful father. What sad luck that our ship was delayed in its leave of harbor. I was presented with a letter the moment I stepped ashore here... I still don't know how he died. The letter didn't mention more than his murder. Though I have my suspicions. Othello: A blackhearted rumor floats around town, my lord. I'd desire you to hear it from a kind voice first. Your sister, perhaps. Laertes: You and I are brothers of a kind. What is this vile rumor? Othello: ... The people whisper he was murdered, my lord. By the King's hand. Laertes: I see. Somehow I can't find it in me to be surprised. Here I assumed that bastard Hamlet would have done the deed. But the King is his blood, and murderers tend to generate more of their kind. With the bastard dead, it's too bad there's no one to ask about it. Lord Laertes... it always was a funny title. What fortunate luck that our ship was delayed in its leave of harbor. I was presented with a letter the moment I stepped ashore here... The letter I received spoke of something horrible. Prince Hamlet made an attempt on my father's life. And now I must repay the deed in kind. Othello: Any honorable man would surely feel the same, my lord. Though the precise interpretation of 'repaying the deed' is subject to some discussion, I should think. After all, the Prince is dead. Laertes: He—Hamlet—is dead? Othello: Yes. It came as a surprise to me, too. Can you not bring him to justice? Laertes: Perhaps. But as things stand, I desire only his death and my family's immediate safety. I have to believe Claudius was behind this somehow. That he ordered Hamlet to come after my father. Hamlet may be a fool, but he wouldn't plot against my father alone. Not without being... pushed. The letter spoke only of 'urgent matters' requiring my attention back at home. Othello: Ah. That'll likely be the Prince, rest his soul. Laertes: He—Hamlet—is dead? Othello: Yes. It came as a surprise to me, too. Laertes: I... I see. I suppose woes spring forth other woes wherever they might land. And I sense more are soon to follow. Othello: Speaking of springing forth... I've heard that Prince Hamlet and Lady Birgitta are to be wed soon. Laertes: Wed? You cannot be serious! Othello: It's a new brand of gossip, my lord, but I believe it trustworthy. The servants who wait upon them both bring swift news to my bar-top. Laertes: Brit... marrying him? Of course the second I depart, Hamlet plots to make her his. The bastard. Othello: Ah, and have you heard the news regarding King Claudius, my lord? He is dead. Laertes: Well, that's certainly news. And what is to become of the throne, then? Othello: They whisper that Hamlet shall rule now. Laertes: What? That incompetent boy? Not if I can help it. Othello: I have heard nothing yet, my lord. Laertes: Fastinating. How can all this have taken place in just two days' time? Othello: I, too, am continually surprised. You Danes are an awfully busy, bloody sort, aren't you. Although I don't know you well, I wish you fortune in whatever you may find when you make your return. Laertes: And I welcome it. I've really no idea what's happening. I suppose I'll soon find out. ... Look at me. Not half a day back from France and all I can think about is murder. The longer I must linger among awful men... The closer I grow to them. Well, fine, then. Let it suit my bloody purpose. It's time. I should have been King. The post was always rightfully mine. Hamlet's mad, the people always hated Claudius... Who better than myself to rule? Time to take what belongs to me.

But the people of Norway have full tables each night, fertile fields in summer, and warm shelter in winter. We do not abandon our sick, our poor, and our old. We care for them. So we do not desire their fear, but rather their continued wealth, and thereby their happiness. Hamlet: Then I grant Denmark to you. Fortinbras: You make the right decision. As a reward for that loyalty, your betrothal to her will stay intact. Lady Birgitta's father has already petitioned me with such an arrangement. source: Bernardo: My men found certain letters in your rooms, Lady Brit, which are written in a most peculiar fashion. At first, simply mundane. A letter to a lady-friend asking her to visit. Then another. Then one to your mother. Birgitta Sophie Brockenhuus. That's your full name, correct? As I've heard it, the roots of the Brockenhuus family run deep. Yours is the Danish branch, but if one traces the generations up the tree, one quickly finds the stock wanders... northward. You seem to write your mother fondly. And you've been sending her drawings of the countryside, haven't you? Brit: I draw. And I paint. Is there harm in that? Bernardo: At first I thought them simple drawings of the world seen from Elsinore's heights. But these are no idle sketches. These are maps. And troop markings. You've passed them information about every stationed man from here to the next northern harbor! For what purpose have you passed this information to your family? Brit: ... If you're waiting for me to cave, we'll be here a long time. Bernardo: Allow me to be frank. Your crime is immutable. But the punishment is yet to be determined. My men have been dispatched to your family's home. I'm confident that by tonight, we'll have our answer, with or without your consent to speak. Brit: Leave my family out of this. I acted alone. Bernardo: That's impossible. I don't believe it for a single moment. I know your father. I know what sort of man he is. Brit: I said, I acted alone. Bernardo: I will not permit you to sign your death warrant yet. I will return tomorrow. Perhaps a night of sleeping on stone will rouse your reason. Then you must bear the full burden of the crime. Lady Birgitta Brockenhuus, I sentence you to die this night. Regardless of any confession you make now—it's too late for that. Brit: The King is in danger. And so are you. Bernardo: What? Brit: Nothing you do can save the throne of Denmark now. Even killing me won't stop the axe from falling. Bernardo: Enough. Brit: Oh... God, please, I don't want to die. Someone, save me from this hell!

source: Quince: A clever little play to put on. To whit, it sends Lady Birgitta scrambling, not that she poses a danger to you anymore. That's a little cruel of you, don't you think? Ophelia: I was curious. Quince: You are 'curious' like a small child holding two halves of an insect between their pinched fingers. Pulling until the insides spill out... yes. Cruel, but ignorant of that cruelty. Ophelia: I'm not ignorant. I'm trying to do everything in my power to find a way around you. Quince: And innocent people are the collateral? Isn't that the very thing you stood against? Don't misunderstand me. I didn't come to insult you. I'm so very pleased to see you doing these sorts of things. It's a funny thing, that play. I edited the timeline—for your benefit, I might add—by telling Lady Brit just one little thing. She and Fortinbras both believed that by eliminating you, Laertes would be driven to seize the throne, and Claudius would fall. But the truth of the matter is, your death is inconsequential! No matter if you are dead or alive, it all crumbles regardless. And by proxy, your very life itself matters not! Until now, you've had such great care for these little humans and their lives. Even after you were nothing to them, after all. So play on, Ophelia. Play all you like. I'll be watching with a smile.
